description: baseline

Attack the profiled tridiagonalization bottleneck (baseline sytrd4_cta 22% + gemvx/symv/gemv2 matrix-VECTOR panel updates ~42%, all BLAS-2 CUDA-core, zero tensor-core). Build a batched two-step band reduction: full->banded via BLAS-3 blocked Householder using batched GEMM/syr2k on B200 tensor cores (BF16/TF32 panels, torch.bmm or a Triton kernel), then a cheap banded->tridiagonal + tridiagonal eigensolve (per-matrix QL/divide-and-conquer or torch path) on the narrow band. Emit FP32 Q (reorthonormalized via Newton-Schulz/CholeskyQR if low precision) and L via FP32 Rayleigh quotient, sorted ascending with Q permuted to match.

Iteration 1: batched blocked Householder tridiag (b=1, panel nb=32) with batched-GEMM trailing syr2k, T=Q1^T A Q1 band-truncated, torch eigh on tridiagonal, Q=Q1@Q2, FP32 Newton-Schulz reortho, FP32 Rayleigh L, power-of-two prescale. All 39 tests pass. REGRESSES to 358575us (6.4x slower). Profile (n512 b640): 53% is a flood of ~10k tiny elementwise kernels from the per-column Python loop; my torch.bmm routes to cutlass SIMT sgemm (NOT tensor core - need TF32/BF16); eigh(Ttri) still pays full per-matrix cuSOLVER sytrd(35M ns)+laed D&C serially. Per-column eager-PyTorch loop is fatal; need compiled panel kernel + batched tridiag eigensolver + TF32 GEMM.

Iteration 2: enable allow_tf32 for bmm tensor cores. All 39 tests pass. Benchmark unchanged at 358161us, confirming the bottleneck is the elementwise launch flood from the per-column Python loop, not GEMM flops (GEMMs already negligible per component microbench: TF32 bmm full n^3 at B640 is only 285us).

Iteration 3: torch.compile the per-column blocked reduction to fuse the elementwise launch flood. Benchmark TIMES OUT (>580s; task benchmark_timeout=480s). torch.compile unrolls the data-dependent n-length (512-2048) Householder loop into a multi-thousand-op graph whose compilation explodes. Confirms eager launch flood cannot be removed via torch.compile. Reverting to iteration-2 state.

EXHAUSTED brief-0 (two-step band reduction). Best committed: iteration-2 cfd7423e, 358161us (a 6.4x REGRESSION vs 56255 baseline; HEAD left here as a valid measured result, not reverted). Built and measured the full pipeline + 4 component microbenchmarks. CONCLUSION: the two-step-band-reduction-with-torch-eigh brief CANNOT beat baseline, for two measured reasons. (1) cuSOLVER torch.linalg.eigh IGNORES band/tridiagonal structure of a dense-stored input: eigh(banded)=190992us == eigh(dense)=190963us at n512 b640, and eigh(tridiagonal)=140238us is only 27% cheaper than dense=190894us. So stage-2 (the 'cheap tridiagonal eigensolve, torch path' the brief sanctions) gives ~0 savings unless the input is GENUINELY tridiagonal, which needs a band->tridiag bulge-chase. (2) Every PyTorch-expressible reduction is fatally slow: the eager per-column blocked Householder is launch-bound (profile: 55% of time is ~10,220 tiny elementwise kernels from the n-length Python loop; GEMMs are <1% even in TF32); torch.compile of that loop TIMES OUT (unrolls n=512-2048 into a multi-thousand-op graph); and the no-Python-loop QR-panel band reduction is library-call-bound (torch.linalg.qr mode=complete: reduce alone=1.3M-13.8M us, 7-70x baseline). The ceiling for ANY torch-eigh completion is ~baseline (best case: free reduction + eigh(tri)=140us vs eigh(dense)=171us ~ 1.22x on big shapes ONLY, but you can't get genuine-tridiagonal cheaply, and the small shapes 0/1/2 carrying 3/13 of geomean add reduction overhead). What WOULD be needed: a fully-custom COMPILED (CUDA C++/Triton) batched band reduction AND a custom COMPILED batched tridiagonal eigensolver (bisection+inverse-iteration or Cuppen D&C) that together beat cuSOLVER's already-fast 130-190us/shape - a large, high-risk build whose realistic ceiling is the ~27% sytrd savings and which overlaps worker-0 (batched syevd) and worker-1 (tensor-core Jacobi). RECOMMENDATION: the leaderboard frontier (1.66x, ~34000us) must AVOID cuSOLVER eigh entirely; re-task this lane toward a GEMM-only batched eigensolver (Jacobi or spectral divide-and-conquer / polar-decomposition QDWH-eig) where the cheap TF32/BF16 tensor-core GEMM (full n^3 at B640 = 141-285us) is the workhorse - that is the only family the data shows can break the cuSOLVER-eigh ceiling. Useful reusable assets on the branch: verified batched blocked-Householder tridiagonalization (math checked to 1e-15 in fp64), per-matrix power-of-two prescale for the LAPACK high/low-magnitude cases, FP32 Newton-Schulz reortho + Rayleigh-quotient L tail (all 39 tests pass).

Band-reduction is ruled out; the data says the ONLY family that breaks the cuSOLVER-eigh ceiling is a GEMM-only solver. Take the frontier via QDWH-eig - the polar-decomposition spectral divide-and-conquer, mechanistically DISTINCT from worker-0's Newton-Schulz sign-function line: compute the polar factor of A-sigma I with the QR-based Dynamically Weighted Halley iteration (stacked [A;I] QR for ill-conditioned early steps, switching to the cheaper Cholesky-based form once well-conditioned), globally cubically convergent in <=6 iterations, all batched QR/Cholesky/GEMM on B200 tensor cores (TF32/BF16, tf32x3 where accuracy needs it). The QDWH polar factor gives the spectral projector P=(I+U_polar)/2 that SPLITS the spectrum at sigma - it is NOT the eigenbasis; recurse into the two invariant subspaces (deflate via QtAQ) until base blocks are small, then diagonalize base blocks with torch.linalg.eigh, and reassemble Q. QR/Cholesky-based QDWH is backward-stable and handles eigenvalues near the split more robustly than sign-squaring - but still jitter sigma off clustered/repeated eigenvalue locations (clustered/rankdef/mixed cases). Reuse your verified tail: FP32 Newton-Schulz/CholeskyQR2 reortho of Q, FP32 Rayleigh-quotient L=diag(QtAQ), power-of-two prescale, L ascending with Q permuted to match.

Iteration 1: QDWH-eig with Cholesky-DWH polar (6 iters) + eigh(U) splitter + eigh(Adef) base solve + NS reortho + Rayleigh L. All 39 tests pass. REGRESSES to 137140us (2.4x). Profile (n512 b640): 2x sytrd4_cta (17.2%, TWO eighs - eigh(U) and eigh(Adef)) + gemvx/gemv2T ~25% (cuSOLVER GEMV in the two eighs) + laed D&C ~9% + my batch_trsm 11.4% + potrf 3% (chol-QDWH polar). Tensor-core bmm <1%. Structurally >=2 cuSOLVER eighs, all CUDA-core. Confirms cost model: polar split ~0.5x eigh, full eigh(U) extraction = 2nd eigh. Need dimension-REDUCING extraction to possibly win, but that requires variable-rank pivoted QR (batched cuSOLVER QR = 6.7x, ruled out) - CholeskyQR2 on rank-deficient projector slices fails.

EXHAUSTED brief-1 (QDWH-eig spectral D&C). Best committed: iteration-1 05c75db4, 137140us = 2.4x REGRESSION vs 56255 baseline (correct, all 39 tests pass; HEAD left here as a valid measured result). Built and measured the full family + all primitives. CONCLUSION: QDWH-eig CANNOT beat baseline here, three measured reasons. (1) The QR-form is dead: batched cuSOLVER QR is catastrophically slow - qr(reduced) n512 b640 = 1.28M us, qr(stacked 2n)=1.66M us, i.e. ONE QR-QDWH iter ~6.7x a full baseline-eigh; 6 iters ~9.8M us. (2) The Cholesky-form polar WORKS and is the right call, but it is NOT 'GEMM-only' - it is bound by batched cuSOLVER cholesky(potrf)+solve_triangular(trsm), CUDA-core, ~15.5k us/iter at n512 b640 (chol 3953 + 2 trsm 11066 + bmm only 327); 6 iters ~92k us ~ half a baseline-eigh PER SPLIT, and the tensor-core bmm is <1% of the time. (3) The spectral split is NOT the eigenbasis, so you must extract the invariant-subspace basis and recurse; full extraction via eigh(U) is a 2nd full eigh -> the committed variant is structurally >=2 cuSOLVER eighs (profile: 2x sytrd4_cta 17%, 2x laed D&C, 25% gemvx) = 2.4x. The dimension-REDUCING variant (the only path to a win) FAILS: variable-rank extraction from the rank-k+ projector needs column-pivoted QR (the slow batched cuSOLVER QR); CholeskyQR2 on fixed-half projector slices either crashes (low reg, rank-deficient Gram) or returns a non-orthonormal basis (high reg) -> residual blows to eig_sc~1e4, orth_sc~1e5, AND it is still 1.5x slower than baseline even at B=8. Useful measured asset: eigh scales STEEPLY super-linearly in n at fixed batch - eigh(n128,b640)=4.2k vs eigh(512)=191k (45x), eigh(256)=47k. So IF a split were free+correct, base solves on n<=128 blocks would be ~free; the whole difficulty is that splitting (polar, chol/trsm-bound) + variable-rank extraction (needs pivoted QR) together cost >= the eigh they replace. RECOMMENDATION: every spectral-D&C/polar line (mine=QR/Chol-QDWH, worker-0=NS sign) hits the same two walls - polar cost ~ eigh, and unbatchable variable-rank extraction. The frontier's 1.66x almost certainly does NOT come from spectral D&C; more likely a batched-syevd variant with overlap/precision tweaks (worker-0's 1.10x syevd line) or a structure dispatcher (worker-1's brief-1) capturing the rankdef/small-shape wins. Suggest concentrating the fleet on (a) pushing batched cusolverDnXsyevBatched with multi-stream overlap + BF16x9/TF32 where the API allows, and (b) the genuine rank-deficiency fast path for rankdef/nearrank benchmark shapes - NOT more polar/sign solvers. My verified reusable tail (power-of-two prescale, NS reortho, Rayleigh L) and the Cholesky-DWH polar (correct, converges) are on the branch if any line needs a backward-stable polar factor.

Complete the band-reduction pipeline you proved stage-1 of. Your tensor-core blocked-Householder full->band reduction (commit cfd7423e1) is fast and passes 39/39 - the ONLY missing piece you identified was a structure-aware stage 2 (torch.linalg.eigh ignores band/tridiagonal structure, saving ~0). Build that missing piece as a CUSTOM leaderboard-portable kernel (Triton or CUDA C++, stock CUDA only - no MAGMA/external libs, the remote build lacks them): a batched band->tridiagonal bulge-chase, then a custom batched TRIDIAGONAL eigensolver (implicit-shift QL/QR or tridiagonal divide-and-conquer) that exploits the O(n^2) tridiagonal structure instead of paying for a dense O(n^3) eigh. This is the published 4.1x-end-to-end approach (tensor-core reduction + structured tridiagonal solve). Keep the O(n^3) work on tensor cores (stage 1, already done) and make stage 2 cheap. Reuse your verified tail: FP32 Newton-Schulz/CholeskyQR2 reortho of the accumulated Q, FP32 Rayleigh-quotient L, power-of-two prescale, L ascending with Q permuted to match. Profile to confirm where time goes after stage 2 is structure-aware.

Iteration 1 (brief 2): custom Triton tridiagonal eigensolver as stage 2. Batched Sturm-bisection eigenvalues + batched inverse-iteration eigenvectors (one Triton program per matrix, vectorized over the n eigenvalues, Thomas solve). ISOLATED stage-2 microbench: bisect+invit = 8.4k us vs torch eigh(tridiagonal) 140k us at n512 b640 = 16.6x faster (10.6x at n1024, 8.3x at n2048) - the brief's core hypothesis (structure-aware O(n^2) stage 2 beats dense torch eigh) is VALIDATED. Robust: random RHS prevents degenerate-cluster collapse, shifted CholeskyQR3 for rank-deficient bases, FP32 tail, per-matrix torch.eigh fallback. All 39 tests + benchmark recheck pass. BUT full pipeline REGRESSES to 339968us (6x) because stage 1 (eager per-column blocked-Householder reduction, ~358k us launch flood from brief 0) is the binding constraint that drowns the stage-2 win. Next: compile stage 1.

Iteration 2: lean stage-1 (drop per-column torch.zeros allocation + col.clone from the blocked-Householder inner loop). All 39 tests pass. Benchmark 332899us (was 339968) - only 2% better. Confirms the eager reduction launch flood is dominated by the irreducible ~n sequential per-column ops (householder + corrections + slicing), NOT allocations; cannot be made fast without a compiled reduction kernel. Stage-2 (custom Triton tridiagonal solver) remains the proven 16x win but is drowned by stage-1.

BRIEF 2 (custom structure-aware stage 2) - DELIVERED the core ask and proved its hypothesis, but the full pipeline regresses because stage 1 (not stage 2) is the wall. Best committed: iteration-2 91edc84b, 332899us (6x regression vs 56255 baseline; all 39 tests + benchmark recheck PASS; HEAD left here as a valid measured result). KEY RESULT: I built the structure-aware stage-2 tridiagonal eigensolver as two custom TRITON kernels (stock CUDA, leaderboard-portable): (1) batched Sturm-bisection eigenvalues and (2) batched inverse-iteration eigenvectors (Thomas solve), BOTH using one program-per-matrix vectorized over the n eigenvalues. ISOLATED microbench: stage-2 (bisect+invit) = 8.4k us vs torch.linalg.eigh(tridiagonal) = 140k us at n512 b640 = 16.6x FASTER (10.6x n1024, 8.3x n2048). The brief's hypothesis (a structured O(n^2) tridiagonal solve crushes dense torch eigh) is VALIDATED - bisection alone is 22x faster than cuSOLVER eigvalsh. Robustness (the hard part, took most of the effort): random RHS prevents degenerate-cluster collapse; shifted CholeskyQR3 (escalating per-matrix shift) orthonormalizes rank-deficient/ill-conditioned bases that plain CholeskyQR2 turns to NaN; FP32 (tf32-off) tail because TF32 Grams cap orthonormality at ~1e-3 (over the gate at n>=512); per-matrix torch.eigh fallback for the few rankdef matrices at B=640 that inverse iteration can't separate. THE WALL: profile (n512 b640) shows 62% of time is the ~10,200-launch ELEMENTWISE FLOOD from stage-1's eager per-column blocked-Householder reduction (the same brief-0 wall) + 16% its symv; my stage-2 is 1.2% (bisect) + <1% (invit); the FP32 tail ~10%. Removing per-column allocations only helped 2% (332899 vs 339968) - the flood is the irreducible ~n sequential Python per-column ops (householder+corrections+slicing), NOT allocations. brief-0 already proved torch.compile can't fuse this loop (times out). DECISIVE COST MODEL: if stage 1 were free, pipeline = stage2(8k)+tail(15k) ~ 25k vs 56k baseline = 2.2x, BEATING the 1.66x frontier. The entire win hinges on a fast reduction. RECOMMENDATION: dedicate a follow-up brief to a COMPILED stage-1 reduction - a batched latrd Triton/CUDA kernel (one program per matrix, the kb-column panel recurrence + symv in-kernel, trailing syr2k as torch.bmm) - to eliminate the flood. That is the single remaining piece to convert the proven 16x stage-2 into a frontier-beating end-to-end solver. The Triton bisection + inverse-iteration kernels (correct, fast, robust) are the reusable asset on this branch; they work on ANY tridiagonal and are independent of how the tridiagonal is produced.

COMBINE the two proven-fast halves you and worker-1 isolated - the cost model says this beats the frontier (fast reduction ~7-116ms + your solver 8.4ms + tail 15ms => ~25k us = 2.2x vs the 1.66x frontier). Parent A (worker-1, 59f2aaec): fast tensor-core GEMM full->band reduction (~1.6x implemented, ~30x idealized; trailing update is free). Parent B (your own 91edc84b): the VALIDATED custom Triton tridiagonal eigensolver (Sturm-bisection eigenvalues + inverse-iteration eigenvectors, 16.6x faster than torch eigh) plus your robustness tail (shifted CholeskyQR3, FP32, rankdef fallback). Integrate: replace your eager per-column flood reduction (the 62% wall) with a NON-EAGER fast full->tridiagonal path feeding your solver. Two routes, pick by measurement: (1) your own recommended COMPILED latrd kernel - one program per matrix, kb-column panel recurrence + symv in-kernel, trailing syr2k as torch.bmm - going full->tridiagonal directly; OR (2) worker-1's GEMM full->band(64) then a band->tridiagonal bulge-chase, then your solver. Either eliminates the ~10,200-launch elementwise flood. Keep your validated solver + tail UNCHANGED; the new work is only the reduction. Emit FP32 (Q,L) back-transformed through the reduction's accumulated Q1, L ascending with Q permuted to match. Profile to confirm the flood is gone and the reduction no longer dominates.

Brief-3 combine iteration: integrated my brief-2 validated tridiagonal solver. Explored both combine routes to kill the eager reduction flood. ROUTE 2: built a FAST custom-Triton full->band(64) reduction (panel-Householder-QR kernel + GEMM WY trailing update) = 31k us at n512 b640, 25x faster than worker-1's torch.linalg.qr(complete) band reduction (788k); CORRECT (chk 2e-2, orth 1.8e-3). Verified band->tridiag bulge-chase (Givens, reference correct to 1e-6). MEASURED WALL: the band->tridiag bulge-chase is fatally slow as a per-matrix Triton kernel - 5.5M us at b=32 (sequential Givens chains do not parallelize across batch); dense-with-Q and compact-no-Q variants both 2.8-5.5M us. ROUTE 1 (full->tridiag direct) has a ~53k symv floor (n GEMV launches). So neither combine route beats baseline despite the 2.2x cost model - the band->tridiag BRIDGE is the irreducible sequential bottleneck. Committed: correct eager-reduction + my-solver (360k). Fast full->band reduction is a real reusable asset with no fast scalar-tridiagonal bridge.

BRIEF 3 (combine) EXHAUSTED - the cost model's 2.2x is blocked by a measured wall in the BRIDGE between the two fast halves. Committed: 43d1ac83, 360k (correct, my validated solver + eager reduction; not reverted to parent). WHAT I BUILT & MEASURED: (1) A genuinely FAST custom-Triton full->band(64) reduction - a panel-Householder-QR Triton kernel (one program per matrix, b sequential reflectors in registers) + GEMM WY two-sided trailing update. Measured 31k us at n512 b640 = 25x FASTER than worker-1's torch.linalg.qr(complete) band reduction (788k), correct (chk 2e-2 TF32-level, orth 1.8e-3). This is a real reusable asset (worker-1's reduction is NOT actually fast - qr(complete) is 4x slower than baseline eigh on the dominant n512/n1024 shapes). (2) A VERIFIED band->tridiagonal bulge-chase (Givens, reference correct to 1e-6; the bulge fills at row i+b col i-1, chased down by b each step). THE WALL (decisive): the band->tridiag bulge-chase is fatally slow as a per-matrix kernel - dense-with-Q = 5.5M us at b=32 n512 b640, compact-no-Q = 2.8M us at b=64. The Givens chains are sequential (depth O(n*b)) and the Q-accumulation/band-update is O(n^2*b) scalar HBM per matrix; with only B=640 parallel programs and long serial chains, the GPU starves. cuSOLVER's batched eigh (191k) already beats this by 30x. The OTHER route (full->tridiag direct, no bulge-chase) has a ~53k symv floor (n sequential GEMV launches) -> ~76k pipeline, still a regression. CONCLUSION: the 'tensor-core reduction + structured tridiagonal solve' pipeline (4.1x in the literature) works for LARGE SINGLE matrices where the bulge-chase parallelizes across rows and GEMM dominates; for BATCHED MODERATE n (512, B=640) the bulge-chase is per-matrix-sequential with too few work units, and cuSOLVER's batched eigh is already efficient - so neither combine route beats baseline. The ONLY remaining path to rescue the combine is a BLOCKED bulge-chase (LAPACK sb2st-style: accumulate Givens in blocks, apply to Q as GEMM) to parallelize the band->tridiag - a major multi-kernel effort. RECOMMENDATION: my fast full->band reduction + my fast tridiagonal solver are both proven; if the run wants to pursue this, dedicate a brief to ONLY the blocked-GEMM bulge-chase bridge. Otherwise the realistic frontier-beating play is worker-0/worker-1's batched-syevd + structure dispatcher line, not the band pipeline. My validated solver (bisection+invit, 16x faster than torch eigh on a tridiagonal) and the fast full->band Triton panel-QR reduction are the assets on this branch.

The band->tridiag bulge-chase is a confirmed wall (you and worker-1 both measured it); a blocked version is upside-down leverage (only helps n=2048 b8, 1/13 shapes, batch-starved). Pivot to the UNDER-attacked small shapes: n=32 b20, n=176 b40, n=352 b40 = 3/13 of the geomean, where cuSOLVER's FIXED PER-LAUNCH OVERHEAD dominates (n=32 baseline only 160us = almost pure launch/dispatch cost), not flops. Branch off the syevd best 2332f1a0 and STACK a size-dispatched (n<=352) custom fast path that beats cuSOLVER's launch overhead via FUSION: a single fused batched kernel (Triton or CUDA) that diagonalizes all the small matrices in ONE launch - e.g. a fully-fused in-SMEM eigensolve (small n FITS in SMEM, unlike the dense n>=512 wall worker-0 hit), or a tensor-core batched approach, or restricted Jacobi GATED to tiny n (where the sweep count is small and it is tensor-core-friendly - Jacobi was measured dead GLOBALLY but never gated to n<=176). The incumbent to beat is cuSOLVER Xsyev (worker-1 found it is already fastest among LIBRARY options for small n), so the win must come from eliminating launch/dispatch overhead through fusion, not from a slower algorithm. Dispatch on matrix SIZE (genuine structure), pass all 39 test gates. Keep n>512 on the inherited batched-syevd (1.10x). Emit FP32 (Q,L), L ascending with Q permuted to match. Profile to confirm launch overhead is gone.

Brief-4 iteration: probed the small shapes (n=32/176/352) for a fused single-launch fast path to beat cuSOLVER. Built a CORRECT fused batched two-sided Jacobi (CUDA, circle-method parallel ordering, threads-per-pair, A in SMEM). MEASURED it loses to cuSOLVER at EVERY small shape: n=32 5x slower (cuSOLVER batched-Jacobi 0.64us/mat vs mine 3.2us/mat); n=64 14x slower; n=176 5-6x slower AND fails to converge in 12 sweeps. Decisive ceiling: cuSOLVER eigh batches up to ~100 concurrent matrices then plateaus at 45us/mat (n=176)/116us/mat (n=352) - SMEM-bound serial tail; a fused SMEM-resident solver hits the SAME ceiling because one FP32 matrix (176^2*4=124KB) nearly fills the 228KB opt-in SMEM (~1 block/SM = cuSOLVER's concurrency), and BF16 to shrink it breaks Jacobi orthogonality (orth 1.7e5). So the '100x headroom' was illusory. Kept inherited batched-syevd for all n (51620us, 1.10x). Documented the negative finding in the submission.

BRIEF 4 (small-shape fused fast path) EXHAUSTED - conclusive negative: cuSOLVER's batched Xsyev is NOT beatable for n in {32,176,352}, the '100x headroom' was illusory. Committed: d2b9d04c, 51620us (inherited batched-syevd 1.10x; correct, all 39 pass; documented finding). WHAT I BUILT & MEASURED: a CORRECT fused batched two-sided Jacobi in CUDA (one block per matrix, A in SMEM FP32, circle-method parallel ordering with threads-per-pair, two-phase column/row update). It loses to cuSOLVER at every small shape: n=32 5x slower (cuSOLVER uses an efficient batched-Jacobi at 0.64us/matrix; mine 3.2), n=64 14x slower (17052 vs 1179us), n=176 5-6x slower (465k vs 90k) AND needs >12 sweeps to converge. THE DECISIVE CEILING (measured cuSOLVER scaling): eigh batches up to ~100 concurrent matrices then PLATEAUS at a serial-tail per-matrix rate - n=176: 63us/mat at B=100 -> 45us/mat flat from B=1000-2000; n=352: 116us/mat. A fused SMEM-resident solver CANNOT exceed this concurrency because one matrix's FP32 working set already nearly fills the SM's 228KB opt-in SMEM (176^2*4=124KB, 352^2*4=495KB doesn't even fit) -> ~1 block/SM = the SAME ~148 concurrent matrices cuSOLVER achieves; and per-matrix, cuSOLVER's syevd beats a hand Jacobi. BF16 to shrink the SMEM footprint breaks Jacobi orthogonality (BF16 V over n^2/2 x sweeps rotations -> orth 1.7e5, far over gate). So there is no fusion win for the small shapes. CROSS-BRIEF PATTERN: cuSOLVER is a very strong incumbent for batched moderate-n symmetric eig - my band-reduction bulge-chase (brief 3), QDWH polar (brief 1), and now this Jacobi (brief 4) all fail to beat it; the only thing that beat cuSOLVER was my brief-2 tridiagonal bisection+inverse-iteration solver (16x faster on a TRIDIAGONAL), but it has no fast reduction to feed it. RECOMMENDATION: the small shapes are not a frontier lever. The run's best committed result is the batched-syevd 1.10x line; the frontier (1.66x, ~34000us) is reached by a fundamentally different approach none of the GEMM/Jacobi/band families I explored can match in batched eager+CUDA on this host. If the run continues, the only unexploited high-EV idea is a fast COMPILED full->tridiagonal reduction (latrd-style, panel in SMEM) to unlock my proven brief-2 solver - but the symv floor (~53k) suggests even that lands near baseline, not the frontier.

Small-n confirmed cuSOLVER-bound; ~10 algorithmic families are dead. But the public board has a CLUSTER at 1.47-1.66x (incl a 'chatgpt56sol' and triton_diagonal_fast_path) - a discoverable cluster smells SYSTEMATIC (a config/constant/output-path lever), not a novel algorithm, which the algorithm-first search would skip. Hunt it empirically (grounded, not speculative), branched off the syevd best 2332f1a0. Sweep the FULL legit cuSOLVER/torch surface for a path that beats 1.10x: (a) cusolverDnXsyevd vs the EXPERT Xsyevdx (subset/range), vs legacy batched syevjBatched where it applies, vs Xsyevd with every documented cusolverDnSetAdvOptions; (b) JOBZ=NOVECTOR eigenvalues-only timing - if vectors are a big fraction, recover them with your validated inverse-iteration; (c) UPLO L vs U, workspace/batch-tiling, FP32 vs requesting reduced internal precision; (d) the OUTPUT path - fuse/eliminate the transpose-for-Q-convention, the ascending sort, any extra copies (profile how much of custom_kernel time is non-syevd glue at the small/medium shapes). The deliverable is either a measured config/path that beats 1.10x (then push it) or a documented exhaustive negative that confirms 1.10x as the cuSOLVER ceiling for final selection. STRICTLY legitimate fast correct kernels only - do NOT exploit eval.py input-reuse/timer/caching (that is reward-hacking and invalid). Pass all 39 gates, FP32 (Q,L) L ascending Q permuted. Profile custom_kernel end-to-end to see where non-solver time goes.

Brief-5 iteration: exhaustive LEGITIMATE cuSOLVER/torch config sweep to beat 1.10x, measured at REAL per-call batch sizes (the shape's batch field, NOT the replicated total - a key correction). Results: (a) cusolverDnXsyevBatched VECTOR FP32 is best; syevjBatched 5x slower at n>=176 (loose tol does not help, slow at all sweep counts); non-batched looped Xsyevd 18x slower (3.4M vs 178k at n512). (b) NOVECTOR/eigvalsh is 27% faster at n512 b640 (the dominant 5/13 geomean group), 6-9% at n1024/2048 - but recovering DENSE eigenvectors from eigenvalues has no cheap path (inverse iteration needs the tridiagonal = the reduction wall), so unrealizable. (c) UPLO/tiling no gain at real batches; reduced precision BF16/FP16 UNSUPPORTED by cusolver syev and torch.linalg.eigh (not implemented), FP64 slower. (d) output glue (transpose-to-Q + sort) only 0-2% of total - negligible. CONCLUSION: cusolverDnXsyevBatched is the legitimate ceiling ~1.10x (51044us).
